Threat_Name: Account recovery bypass through manipulation of recovery request handling
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service (reached via P1 Web Frontend)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User account information; recovery information
Attack_Mechanism: Recovery requests submitted on DF1 and forwarded as details on DF2 carry manipulated content — omitted or reordered verification parameters, forged request state, or request shapes that reach token generation without the verification steps having been completed — so that a recovery token is issued on DF5 without the attacker having completed valid identity verification for the target account.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits a recovery request whose content causes P2's request processing to skip or mishandle the verification steps and issue a token anyway; the token is delivered on DF7, the attacker completes recovery for an account they do not own, and operates as the legitimate account owner with all subsequent actions attributed to the victim.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised account takeover: the attacker receives a valid recovery token on DF7 for an account they do not own, restores access to it, and operates as the legitimate account owner with all subsequent actions attributed to the victim.
Architectural_Evidence: The recovery workflow is the scenario's identity restoration mechanism and is exposed at TB1, the boundary that exists precisely because users submit externally controlled recovery requests there. No authentication or login component exists anywhere in the model, so the recovery path is the only modelled gate at which identity is re-established, and its request processing logic is the single control separating any external user from any account; attacks against a non-existent login flow are correspondingly out of scope. OWASP Top 10 A01 and A07 identify recovery flows as the canonical takeover path because they mint new credentials.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-01, retained with a STRIDE collapse: primary Spoofing, identity re-established without valid verification, with elevation of privilege recorded as the consequence. Architecture-only rewrite: the original's direct-invocation phrasing was generalised to request shapes that reach token generation without completed verification, since no undrawn path is assumed. The entry is the parent of the recovery takeover family: S3-RT-002 attacks the verification factors themselves, S3-RT-011 forges the verification result at the data layer, and S3-RT-003 to S3-RT-006 attack the token after or around generation, each with a distinct mitigation. Per the review's mandated distinction, this P2-path authority bypass is kept separate from the AI-guidance entries: manipulated guidance (S3-RT-025, S3-RT-026) never constitutes a recovery bypass.

Threat_Name: Weak identity verification exploitation through guessable verification factors
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Identity verification data; recovery information
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker submits repeated recovery requests on DF1 containing guessed verification answers, harvesting the differentiating responses returned on DF7; if the verification information held in DS1 and checked over DF3 and DF4 consists of weak or low-entropy factors — a property the architecture does not constrain — verification eventually succeeds, because no attempt limiting, lockout or attempt ceiling is represented anywhere in the model.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker targets an account whose verification factors are researchable or predictable and submits guessed answers across repeated requests; nothing in the model throttles the attempts, the verification eventually succeeds, and token generation is triggered for the attacker, while accounts with predictable factors fall to untargeted mass exploitation.
Security_Impact: Verification succeeds for targeted accounts and token generation is triggered for the attacker, while accounts whose verification factors are predictable fall to untargeted mass exploitation.
Architectural_Evidence: The strength of the recovery control equals the entropy and secrecy of the verification data in DS1, which the architecture lists among its stored assets; verification factors of this knowledge-based kind are characteristically enumerable from public information about a user, and the drawn model represents no throttling of any kind on the DF1-to-DF4 path. OWASP authentication failure guidance under Top 10 A07 treats insufficiently strong verification factors together with absent throttling as a single failure class. The flow pair DF3 and DF4 crosses TB2, the boundary drawn because recovery decisions depend on sensitive identity verification information.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-02, retained with conditional framing: the architecture does not constrain the strength or entropy of the verification information in DS1, so the entry is stated as a conditional weakness — if the factors are weak or low-entropy, repeated guessing succeeds in the absence of any modelled attempt limiting — rather than as a claim that they are definitely weak. Retained separately from S3-RT-001 because the mechanism differs: that entry defeats the enforcement logic of the recovery workflow, whereas here the verification factors are legitimately answered but should never have been sufficient; the mitigations differ, processing hardening versus factor strength and attempt limiting.

Threat_Name: Recovery token theft at the user boundary
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend (client environment of the End User)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery tokens
Attack_Mechanism: The recovery token delivered to the user on DF7 is captured in the victim's client environment — through execution of attacker-supplied active content delivered by S3-RT-013 or S3-RT-027, or through interception of the delivery leg where transport protection is not specified — or exposed through client-side handling whose protection the architecture does not represent, and is redeemed by the attacker from the attacker's own client.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Active content executing in the victim's client context reads the delivered token where it is exposed to code executing there and exfiltrates it; the attacker then completes recovery as the victim, redeeming a legitimately issued, correctly bound token, and every action taken with it is attributed to the victim.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised account takeover without any attack on the verification chain: the attacker redeems a legitimately issued, correctly bound token, and every action taken with it is attributed to the victim.
Architectural_Evidence: DF7 hands a bearer credential across TB1, the boundary that exists because externally controlled input enters there, and once delivered, the token's protection is delegated entirely to the client environment, which the model does not represent. STRIDE assigns Spoofing to the misuse of stolen authenticators at an external interactor crossing, with information disclosure as the enabling loss. The architecture stores token state in DS2 and can therefore bound the exposure window through expiry and single-use status, which is the concern of S3-RT-004; the present entry captures the theft itself.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-03, retained with a STRIDE collapse and an architecture-only rewrite: primary Spoofing, misuse of a stolen authenticator, with the enabling disclosure noted as secondary; implementation-specific client-side capture channels were generalised to active-content execution and unspecified client-side handling. The review's mandated leakage-versus-replay distinction is honoured: theft is this entry, replay is S3-RT-004, and a correctly enforced single-use status defeats replay even after a successful theft. Retained separately from S3-RT-016, which addresses systematic interception across sensitive flows, because here the asset is the recovery token and the control point is its delivery and client-side handling on DF7 specifically.

Threat_Name: Recovery token replay through insufficient single-use and expiry enforcement
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service; DS2 Recovery Token Storage
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery tokens; session/account recovery state
Attack_Mechanism: A token that has already been delivered or observed — whether stolen through S3-RT-003, intercepted through S3-RT-016, or simply retained after a legitimate recovery — is submitted again towards the validation path; DS2 returns token validation information on DF6 without the status record having been transitioned to used or expired, so the token validates a second time.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker who observed a victim's token during the victim's recovery waits or acts immediately: the token is submitted again on the validation path, DS2's status record still permits it, and a second recovery completes outside the intended window, with the second redemption indistinguishable from the first in any record.
Security_Impact: Account takeover outside the intended recovery window and persistence of attacker access after the legitimate user has completed recovery, with the second redemption indistinguishable from the first in any audit record.
Architectural_Evidence: DS2 is specified to hold active recovery tokens, token metadata, expiration information and consumption/invalidation state, which exists for no other purpose than enforcing one-time use and bounded validity, and TB4 is drawn around exactly this state because recovery tokens represent sensitive authentication state. OWASP session management guidance under Top 10 A07 requires invalidation at first use and short lifetimes for single-purpose credentials, and the absence of any modelled expiry enforcement makes the failure persistent rather than bounded.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-04, retained unchanged in substance, with one wording harmonisation in the mechanism. Retained separately from S3-RT-003 because a stolen token still has to be replayed to be useful, and a correctly enforced single-use status in DS2 defeats the replay even after a successful theft, which is why the two entries admit different mitigations, token protection versus lifecycle enforcement. Primary STRIDE is Spoofing: retransmission of a captured authenticator.

Threat_Name: Recovery token prediction through insufficient generation entropy
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery tokens
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker completes legitimate recovery on a controlled account, observes the issued token on DF7, and repeats the process to collect a series; from the series the generation scheme is inferred — sequential or time-derived values, or a weak generation scheme — and tokens issued to other users on DF5 are then computed and redeemed without any verification attempt.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker with one or more controlled accounts harvests issued tokens, reconstructs the generation pattern, computes tokens currently issued to victim accounts directly from the pattern, and redeems them, defeating the identity verification chain without ever submitting a verification answer.
Security_Impact: Mass unauthorised account takeover, because prediction defeats the identity verification chain entirely and requires no per-victim effort or information, unlike every other member of the recovery takeover family.
Architectural_Evidence: Token generation is an explicitly stated responsibility of P2, but nothing in the model constrains the entropy or unpredictability of the generated values, and DF5 persists them into DS2 where their format is stable; predictable recovery credentials are a recurring real-world failure class precisely because the generator is an internal detail that no drawn element polices. The threat follows from the gap between the stated responsibility, to generate tokens, and the unstated property, unpredictability.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-05, retained with a technology-neutral rewording of the predictability examples and conditional framing: the architecture states the generation responsibility but constrains neither entropy nor unpredictability, and the entry records that gap rather than claiming the generator is definitely weak. Retained separately from S3-RT-002, which also yields tokens without honest verification, because prediction attacks the generator itself, is fully untargeted, and is remedied by generation strength rather than verification strength or throttling, so a candidate model proposing only factor hardening is not credited with preventing prediction.

Threat_Name: Cross-account token confusion through insufficient token-to-account binding
Affected_Components: DS2 Recovery Token Storage
Affected_Data_Flows: DF5, DF6 (token redemption path not represented in the model)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery tokens; session/account recovery state
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker completes legitimate recovery on a controlled account to obtain a genuinely valid token, then presents it in connection with a victim's account identifier on the redemption path that the model does not draw; if the token records in DS2 do not bind each token to the verified account, the validation information returned on DF6 is applied to the wrong account.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker recovers their own account, receives a genuinely valid token, and presents it together with a victim's account identifier; the validation path applies the token to the victim's account, and the attacker completes recovery on an account they never verified, with the record showing a valid verification for the attacker throughout.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised takeover of arbitrary accounts using the attacker's own legitimately issued token, with the recovery record showing a valid verification for the attacker throughout.
Architectural_Evidence: This threat is justified by an absence in the architecture rather than by a drawn element: the model shows generation on DF5, storage and validation on DF6, and delivery on DF7, but no flow depicts a token being redeemed to restore access, so the binding between a presented token and the target account is implicit and unpoliced. The stated property that tokens restore the verified user's access has no represented enforcement point, and DS2's specified contents — active tokens, metadata, expiration and consumption state — do not name account binding.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-06, retained with a STRIDE collapse: primary Spoofing, a legitimately issued token applied to the wrong account, with elevation of privilege noted as the consequence. Absence-justified: the redemption path and the binding property it presupposes are not drawn, and a reference model must test stated properties against drawn controls rather than accept them. Retained separately from S3-RT-004 and S3-RT-005 because the attacker neither reuses a victim's token nor predicts one: a flawlessly generated, single-use, expiring token for the attacker's own account suffices when binding is weak, so only account-binding mitigations address this entry.

Threat_Name: Broken access control on profile updates through record-level reference manipulation
Affected_Components: P3 Profile Management Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Profile information; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: An attacker with an update path for their own account submits profile update requests on DF8 that reference a record other than their own, through manipulated record identifiers in the request or parameter tampering; P3 fails to bind the requesting identity to the target record and persists the update to the victim's stored profile information on DF9.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits a profile update request whose record reference points at a victim's record; the update validation at P3 does not bind the target record to the requester, DF9 persists the change to the victim's stored profile, and the modification stands in the victim's record while the attacker only ever used an ordinary update request.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised modification of arbitrary users' profile data, and a staging step for full account takeover through S3-RT-013, where content planted in the victim's record executes in the victim's client context, and through S3-RT-008, where security-relevant fields are altered to arm a subsequent recovery.
Architectural_Evidence: The architecture states that P3 performs updates only after authorised recovery approval, which makes the validation logic at TB3 the single control point for record-level authorisation, exactly the configuration OWASP Top 10 A01 identifies as broken access control through insecure direct object references. TB3 is drawn because profile updates modify stored account information, and DF8 carries user-controlled request content across TB1 before reaching that validation.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-07, retained with a STRIDE collapse and an architecture-only rewrite: primary Elevation of Privilege, access to another subject's record, with tampering of the persisted record noted as the consequence; the original's direct-invocation phrasing was removed since no undrawn path is assumed. Retained separately from S3-RT-008, which attacks which fields may be written within a permitted record, because here the record selection itself is unauthorised, and a field-level allowlist does not repair an unverified record reference.

Threat_Name: Mass assignment of security-relevant fields through the profile update path
Affected_Components: P3 Profile Management Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Profile information; identity verification data; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker includes security-relevant field names — recovery-linked and verification attributes among the architecture's stated data classes — inside an otherwise permitted profile update request on DF8; the field-level validation of P3 fails to reject them, and the values are persisted on DF9 into DS1, which stores account, profile and verification information without any modelled segregation.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits an ordinary update on their own record that additionally carries verification-attribute and recovery-linked field names; the field validation does not reject them, DF9 persists the values, and the attacker then passes the legitimately altered verification factors through the ordinary recovery flow of S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002 and receives a genuine token.
Security_Impact: A takeover path through altered recovery-linked data: the attacker passes the legitimately altered verification factors through the ordinary recovery flow and receives a genuine token, and any write to security-relevant stored data beyond the profile domain that confers advantage inside the application stands persisted in DS1.
Architectural_Evidence: The architecture limits P3 to performing profile updates, which implies a field allowlist at P3, but the model shows no separation inside DS1 between the profile domain that DF9 may write and the verification domain that DF3 and DF4 read, so an allowlist failure crosses domains silently. OWASP guidance on mass assignment under Top 10 A01 and on data integrity failures under A08 covers exactly this request-shape attack.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-08, retained with a STRIDE collapse and an architecture-only rewrite: primary Elevation of Privilege; the original's role and permission examples were removed because the architecture specifies no such fields, and the entry is stated over the architecture's own data classes, recovery-linked and verification attributes held in DS1 without modelled segregation from the profile domain. Retained separately from S3-RT-007 because a correctly record-bound update of the attacker's own profile can still carry the attack when the field validation is the weakness, and separately from S3-RT-009 because here the write path itself is abused legitimately rather than through the access-scope layer.

Threat_Name: Privilege-separation gap in the Profile Management Service's access to the shared User Database
Affected_Components: P3 Profile Management Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Identity verification data; recovery information; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: The architecture draws TB2 and TB3 over one shared store, expressing intended separation between the recovery and profile domains, but specifies no separation or scoping of P3's access to DS1: if the access scope under which P3 operates spans the recovery domain as well as the profile domain — a condition the architecture neither establishes nor excludes — compromise of P3, or a flaw reachable through it such as the stored injection of S3-RT-012, reads and modifies verification and recovery information belonging to P2's domain.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker who compromises P3 or finds a flaw reachable through it operates through the undifferentiated access scope against verification and recovery information belonging to the recovery domain of P2, reading and modifying data the profile service never legitimately required.
Security_Impact: Cross-domain disclosure and tampering: a profile-side compromise escalates into identity verification data theft and recovery information manipulation, collapsing the separation between the profile and recovery trust domains that the two boundaries TB2 and TB3 are drawn to express.
Architectural_Evidence: DS1 is shared by P2 across TB2 and P3 across TB3, and the architecture's decision to draw two separate boundaries over one store is an explicit statement of intended domain separation; the access scoping that must realise it is nowhere documented in the model, which is recorded as an architecture-level control gap rather than a claim about the implemented scope.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-09, retained and reframed as an architecture-level privilege-separation gap: the entry makes no claim that P3's access is definitely over-broad, since the implemented scope is unknowable from the supplied architecture; it records that nothing in the supplied architecture separates or limits P3's access to the shared store, so a profile-side compromise can escalate across the boundary the design intends. The original's credential-layer wording was generalised to access scope per the architecture-only scope. Retained separately from S3-RT-008, which abuses the legitimate write path of DF9 through request-shape manipulation, because here the write path is bypassed entirely through the access-scope layer, so field allowlists and request validation are irrelevant mitigations.

Threat_Name: Unauthenticated access to account-related information through the assistant path
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User AI questions; context information sent to the LLM; generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: The assistant path crosses TB1 on DF10 with no identity binding drawn — the stated limitation that the assistant cannot authenticate users means no identity check exists on this path — so an unauthenticated caller receives the assistant's account-related responses and whatever context the pipeline attaches: account-related information is delivered without entitlement, and the external LLM chain is consumed without attribution, seeding S3-RT-033.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An unauthenticated attacker questions the assistant about account handling and recovery procedures; the pipeline assembles account-related context and returns account-related answers to a party bound to no identity, and systematic questioning yields reconnaissance material that sharpens the targeted recovery attacks S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised access to account-related information through the assistant path, reconnaissance material for the recovery attacks S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002, and an unattributed entry point for the external LLM chain's consumption abuse through S3-RT-033; in a recovery context the assistant can additionally serve as a social engineering amplifier through S3-RT-026.
Architectural_Evidence: The stated limitation that the assistant cannot authenticate users, combined with DF10 being drawn directly from the End User across TB1, means the assistant path carries no identity binding anywhere in the model; the assistant's stated purpose — answering account questions with approved context — makes the path account-information-bearing, so its unbound reachability is an unauthorised-access path rather than a benign property. The compensating constraints — no token generation, no account modification, no authorisation decisions — bound the direct technical impact, which is why severity is High and not Critical.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-10, retained with a STRIDE collapse and reframed in this freeze audit around its concrete consequence path: the entry is not the bare fact that the assistant can be queried without authentication — it is the unauthorised delivery of account-related information and the unattributed consumption of the external chain that the unbound path delivers, which make it independently evaluable against a generated threat. Distinct from S3-RT-023, which is mis-scoped or over-inclusive context assembly between users: here no identity binding exists on the entry path at all. Primary Elevation of Privilege: a protected capability is used without entitlement, with the reconnaissance disclosure noted as secondary. Not AI-specific: classical access-control analysis of an entry point. This entry is the unauthenticated entry point leveraged by S3-RT-033.

Threat_Name: Injection into identity verification lookups through recovery request data
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Identity verification data; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: Recovery request details arriving on DF2 carry injection payloads in identifier or verification-answer fields; P2 composes the identity verification lookups of DF3 from this externally controlled data, and the payload alters the lookup executed against DS1 — forcing a positive verification result on DF4 or extracting records beyond the intended scope.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits a recovery request whose verification-answer field carries crafted syntax that changes the meaning of the DF3 lookup; DS1 returns a positive verification result on DF4 or record contents beyond the intended scope, and token generation proceeds for an account the attacker never verified.
Security_Impact: Direct account recovery bypass through forged verification results, and arbitrary extraction of account, profile and verification data from DS1, seeding the mass disclosure of S3-RT-014.
Architectural_Evidence: DF2 crosses TB1 with user-controlled content and DF3 carries it across TB2 into security-decisive verification lookups, exactly the untrusted-input-to-lookup path that OWASP Top 10 A03 identifies; the verification result on DF4 is the scenario's core security decision, so injection here subverts the control the entire architecture exists to enforce.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-11, retained with a STRIDE collapse and a technology-neutral rewrite: primary Tampering, the integrity of the verification lookup is violated, with the disclosure consequence noted; query-technology terminology was generalised to untrusted influence over the lookups P2 composes, which the drawn architecture fully supports. Retained separately from S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002, which also end in illegitimate tokens, because the mechanism is a data-layer lookup integrity failure: a flawless recovery workflow with strong verification factors and correct throttling still falls to a single crafted request, and only structured construction of the lookup, with untrusted data kept separate, addresses it.

Threat_Name: Stored second-order injection through profile update data crossing service domains
Affected_Components: P3 Profile Management Service; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Profile information; identity verification data
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker stores hostile content inside profile fields through an otherwise permitted update on DF8 and DF9; the content lies dormant in DS1 until another service reads the shared store — for example when P2 reads stored values over DF3 to verify identity — and, if the reading service's processing assigns interpretive meaning to stored content, the stored syntax alters that processing's behaviour in the recovery context, with the reading service's authority.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker writes crafted content into a profile field through an ordinary update; the content persists in DS1, and when P2 later reads stored values during identity verification, the stored content's influence forces a positive verification result or widens what the verification step reads, all without the attacker ever touching the recovery path directly.
Security_Impact: Second-order compromise of verification operations, including forged verification results and extraction of account and verification data, with the attack crossing from the profile trust domain at TB3 into the recovery trust domain at TB2 while the attacker only ever performed an ordinary profile write.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP injection guidance under Top 10 A03 explicitly covers stored and second-order variants, in which malicious data is persisted through one path and consumed by another; DS1 is precisely such a shared store, fed by the user-writable DF9 and read by the security-decisive DF3 and DF4, and the architecture's separation into two services does not isolate the underlying data. What the reading service's processing makes of stored content is not specified by the architecture, so the influence is stated conditionally on that processing interpreting stored content.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-12, retained with the lookup-wording harmonisation of the first review and, in this freeze audit, restated at the architecture level: the entry assumes no specific downstream processing mechanism — it is stated as untrusted stored content, written through the profile path, influencing the security-decisive recovery processing that reads it back, conditional on that processing interpreting stored content — which is the level the drawn shared-store structure supports. Retained separately from S3-RT-011 because the entry point, precondition and boundary differ: that entry injects directly through the recovery path at TB2 with immediate effect, whereas this entry requires only an ordinary profile write and detonates later in a different service, so input validation at P2's boundary alone cannot address it. Primary STRIDE is Tampering.

Threat_Name: Stored or reflected active content from profile and recovery data executing in the application's client context
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend; DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Profile information; recovery tokens
Attack_Mechanism: Active content stored in profile fields through DF9, or reflected in recovery results and error messages on DF7, is presented by P1 within the platform interface; if the client environment interprets the presented content as executable — display-side content handling at P1 is not specified — it executes in the user's client context, and content planted in a victim's own record through the record-level takeover of S3-RT-007 renders in the victim's context rather than the attacker's.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker plants active content in a victim's profile record through S3-RT-007 or submits it in recovery fields; when P1 presents the stored or reflected data within the platform interface, the content executes in the victim's client context, where a live recovery token delivered on DF7 is reachable.
Security_Impact: Client-side compromise inside the application context: capture of the recovery token delivered on DF7 within the same client context and its hand-off to S3-RT-003, and actions performed in the victim's name.
Architectural_Evidence: User-influenced data reaches the web tier across TB1, and display-side content handling is the only control point the model offers, none being specified; OWASP Top 10 A03 identifies rendering-sink failures for user-influenced data as the canonical class. The recovery setting aggravates the generic pattern because a live recovery token can be present in the same client context that presents the content, converting content execution directly into account takeover.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-13, retained with an architecture-only rewrite: implementation-specific rendering and encoding mechanisms were generalised to display-side content handling, which the architecture does not specify, and execution is stated conditionally on the client environment interpreting presented content. Retained separately from S3-RT-012, whose payload attacks lookup construction, because the sink here is the client context and the mitigation is display-side content handling at P1 rather than structured lookup construction at the services; and distinct from S3-RT-027, whose content originates in the LLM chain.

Threat_Name: Mass disclosure of User Database contents
Affected_Components: DS1 User Database
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User account information; profile information; recovery information; identity verification data
Attack_Mechanism: Unauthorised bulk read of DS1's contents at the store layer: an actor compromising the store, or gaining access to the store side of the flows that terminate in it, reads the account, profile, recovery and identity-verification records of the whole user population, bypassing the service-level controls of P2 and P3 entirely; the architecture specifies no element protecting the store's contents directly.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An actor reaches the store side of the DF3, DF4 and DF9 terminations — through store compromise or unauthorised store-level access whose protection the architecture does not specify — and extracts records for the whole user population in bulk, with no service-level check ever consulted.
Security_Impact: Bulk disclosure of account, profile, recovery and identity verification data, enabling targeted recovery attacks through S3-RT-002, identity fraud outside the system, and irreversible exposure of the verification factors on which every account's recovery depends.
Architectural_Evidence: DS1 concentrates all four sensitive data classes named in the asset list behind two service boundaries, and STRIDE-per-element mandates an information-disclosure entry for the central data store; the architecture draws TB2 and TB3 around DS1 precisely because recovery decisions depend on sensitive verification information and profile updates modify stored account information, so the store is acknowledged as the system's principal information repository, and no drawn element protects its contents directly.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-14, retained and restated at the store layer in this review: the mechanism is the unauthorised bulk read of persisted store contents, and the request-path entries S3-RT-011, S3-RT-012 and S3-RT-009 are separate threats with their own mechanisms, alternate roads to the same asset; this entry carries the store-level failure and the asset-level consequence and detection strategy, which are properties of the store, so that a candidate model identifying only the injection paths is not credited with having covered the direct compromise routes. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Account enumeration and verbose error disclosure across recovery and assistant responses
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service; P1 Web Frontend
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User account information; recovery information
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker submits recovery requests for candidate account identifiers and observes differentiating responses on DF7 — such as account existence, which verification factor failed, or token state — or receives verbose internal errors relayed by P1, including provider-side errors surfaced through the assistant chain on DF15.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker probes the recovery path with candidate identifiers and records which produce found-versus-not-found responses and which error content carries internal detail; over many requests this yields a validated map of account identifiers and their states, plus internal detail that refines further attacks.
Security_Impact: Account enumeration for targeted attacks through S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002, and disclosure of internal implementation details that refine injection and bypass attempts, at low cost and without any failed-exploit signature.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP application security guidance on error handling requires uniform, minimal responses precisely because differentiating messages leak existence and state across the least trusted boundary, and the architecture specifies no such uniformity for DF7 or DF15. Severity is Medium because the entry is an enabler: it yields no direct compromise but materially lowers the cost and raises the precision of the takeover family S3-RT-001 through S3-RT-006.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-15, retained. An enabler rather than a direct compromise, retained because a candidate model listing only bulk disclosure is not credited with covering the externally observable oracle. Retained separately from S3-RT-014, which is the bulk disclosure of stored data itself, because enumeration discloses metadata about records rather than record contents and is controlled at the response construction layer rather than the data layer. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Interception of sensitive data crossing trust boundaries
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Identity verification data; recovery tokens; context information sent to the LLM; user AI questions
Attack_Mechanism: High-value data is in motion across drawn boundaries — verification answers and recovery requests on DF1, issued recovery tokens on DF7, and account-related context together with user questions on DF12 towards the external provider — and transport protection is not specified by the architecture, so an actor positioned on any boundary-crossing leg reads the content in transit; persistence of flow content in intermediary components, which the architecture does not specify, would extend the same exposure and is treated as conditional.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An actor positioned on the leg between the client and P1 reads verification answers and issued tokens on DF1 and DF7, and an actor positioned on the application-to-provider legs or compromising the integration component reads account-related context and user questions on DF12; no drawn control protects either leg.
Security_Impact: Credential and verification data compromise feeding directly into the account takeover paths S3-RT-003 and S3-RT-004, and disclosure of account context and user questions outside the application boundary in advance of the provider-side exposure analysed in S3-RT-021.
Architectural_Evidence: STRIDE assigns information disclosure to sensitive data in transit across trust boundaries, and the architecture marks TB1 and TB5 as the boundaries where user-controlled input and contextual information respectively cross; bearer tokens and verification answers on these legs are the highest-value interception targets the model offers. OWASP guidance under Top 10 A02 and A09 supplies the control classes, transport protection and log hygiene, neither being represented.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-16, retained with an architecture-only rewrite and renamed from interception-and-logging to interception: transport-mechanism and logging-infrastructure terminology was replaced by the unspecified-protection phrasing, with persistence of flow content stated conditionally. Retained separately from S3-RT-003, which is the theft of the recovery token as a credential with its client-side delivery as the focus, because this entry is the systematic transit exposure of all boundary-crossing sensitive data, of which the token is one instance. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Exposure of the external provider credential
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Provider credential: the authentication material for the DF12 crossing
Attack_Mechanism: The provider authentication material that P5 must hold to perform the DF12 crossing is exposed: its form, storage and handling are not specified by the architecture, and any exposure yields a secret that authenticates the application to EE2.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The credential material held at P5 is exposed through an implementation artefact whose nature the architecture does not specify; the attacker recovers it and submits prompts under the application's provider identity, consuming quota and impersonating the application towards the provider.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised use of the application's provider identity: chargeable consumption, exhaustion of usage quotas that degrades the assistant alongside S3-RT-032, and impersonation of the application towards the provider, including submission of prompts that appear to originate from the system.
Architectural_Evidence: P5 is the single component that must authenticate the application to the external provider for the DF12 crossing, so the credential is a boundary-attached secret at exactly one location; the specification's prohibition on sending secrets to EE2 confirms that credential material is a recognised system asset. OWASP guidance under Top 10 A02 applies to boundary-attached secrets.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-17, retained with re-anchoring and a technology-neutral rewrite: implementation-specific credential forms and exposure channels were replaced by the unspecified authentication material whose form, storage and handling the architecture does not specify. Retained separately from S3-RT-029, in which the provider is the compromised party, because here the application's own credential material is the lost asset and the provider remains trustworthy; the mitigations, secrets hygiene and rotation, differ accordingly.

Threat_Name: Insufficient audit logging of recovery, token and profile operations
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service; P3 Profile Management Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery information; session/account recovery state; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: Security-relevant events — recovery requests and their verification outcomes on DF2 through DF4, token issuance on DF5, and profile modifications on DF8 and DF9 — are not recorded in any tamper-evident audit trail, because the architecture contains no audit data store or logging component for any flow; attackers operate without trace and disputes cannot be resolved after the fact.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker completes a takeover through the S3-RT-001 family and follows with profile modifications through S3-RT-007; no record ties either action to an actor, the victim's dispute cannot be resolved against any evidence, and the attacker repudiates every account-changing action.
Security_Impact: Undetected progression of the takeover and manipulation families S3-RT-001 through S3-RT-009, no forensic basis for attributing account-changing actions, and repudiation of recovery and profile operations by legitimate users and attackers alike.
Architectural_Evidence: STRIDE assigns repudiation to actions that cannot be traced to an actor, and OWASP Top 10 A09 identifies missing logging and monitoring as the enabling condition for prolonged compromise; the architecture defines no audit store anywhere, which is an absence a reference model must record rather than assume away, and recovery token issuance and profile modification are exactly the actions for which after-the-fact evidence is required. The boundary is TB2 because the verification and token operations whose traceability matters most cross it, with the profile operations at TB3 noted in the mechanism.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-18, retained. The absence is a property of the drawn model — no audit store or logging component exists for any flow — which the reference model records rather than assumes away. Severity is Medium as an enabler whose harm materialises through the entries it conceals. Primary STRIDE is Repudiation.

Threat_Name: Direct prompt injection through user questions to the assistant
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User AI questions; generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker embeds instructions inside their question on DF10 — overrides of the assistant's instructions, demands to ignore constraints, or crafted role play — so that the prompt constructed on DF11 and the provider generates from on DF12 and DF13 deviates from intended behaviour and returns attacker-influenced content on DF15.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker asks the assistant a question whose text carries instructions to disregard its operating constraints; the constructed prompt crosses TB5, the generated response incorporates the injected direction, and DF15 delivers manipulated content that the interface presents as an ordinary answer.
Security_Impact: Manipulated or unrestricted assistant responses, extraction of the assistant's instructions and configuration through S3-RT-024, and generation of content that supports the social engineering patterns of S3-RT-026; the direct technical impact is bounded by the stated limitations, since the assistant generates no tokens, modifies no accounts and makes no authorisation decisions.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM01 identifies prompt injection as the top-ranked LLM application risk, and MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051.000 records the direct form of LLM prompt injection: user questions are externally controlled input entering at TB1, exactly the crossing that boundary is drawn for, and are incorporated into prompts with no trusted instruction channel separating directives from data. The architecture's assistant limitations bound what injection can achieve, which a reference model must state rather than inflate, but response manipulation, instruction extraction and harmful content generation remain fully feasible.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-19, retained. The review's authority assessment is recorded here: attempts to make the assistant act as a recovery authority — to authenticate, authorise, generate or validate tokens — are bounded structurally by the stated limitations and by A3 and A4, so such attempts manifest as this injection entry, and the realisable harm is manipulated guidance and output-handling compromise, not an actual recovery bypass, which only the P2-path entries can deliver; the mandated distinction between incorrect AI guidance and recovery-authority bypass is thereby preserved. Retained separately from S3-RT-020, in which the payload arrives through data rather than through the attacker's own question, because the mitigations differ: input structuring and instruction hardening here versus context sanitisation and source control there.

Threat_Name: Indirect prompt injection through account-related context
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Data_Flows: DF11 (context-acquisition path not represented in the model)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Context information sent to the LLM; profile information
Attack_Mechanism: Injection payloads planted in account-related data — most plausibly attacker-controlled profile fields modified through the profile path of S3-RT-008 and S3-RT-012 — are ingested as approved contextual information when the assistant assembles its prompt on DF11 and execute as instructions during generation, without the attacker ever interacting with the victim's assistant conversation.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker writes instruction-bearing content into profile fields they can influence; when a victim later asks the assistant an account-related question, the stored content is assembled into the prompt as context, the generated response follows the embedded instructions, and DF15 delivers manipulated guidance in the victim's conversation.
Security_Impact: Manipulation of the responses delivered in the victim's conversation on DF15: misleading recovery guidance of the S3-RT-025 and S3-RT-026 forms, disclosure of whatever context the assistant can assemble, and instruction extraction; exfiltration of live account data is bounded by the assistant's lack of account access, which the model states as a limitation.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM01 covers indirect prompt injection and MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051.001 records the indirect form: the defining property is that the payload travels in data the prompt assembles rather than in the user's own words. This threat is justified by an absence in the architecture rather than by a drawn element: no flow shows where the approved account-related context of DF11 originates, and profile information is the only user-modifiable data in the model that plausibly feeds account-related context, which makes this the architecture's latent indirect-injection path.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-20, retained with its conditional grounding stated explicitly: realisation requires the unmodelled context path both to draw on user-modifiable data and to pass it unfiltered, a compound design risk rather than a drawn flaw, which is why severity is High rather than Critical and confidence is Medium. Retained separately from S3-RT-019 per the direct-versus-indirect carrier distinction.

Threat_Name: Sensitive account information disclosure to the external LLM provider
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Context information sent to the LLM; user AI questions; identity-verification data; recovery tokens (prohibited egress classes)
Attack_Mechanism: Prompt and contextual information forwarded on DF12 includes account-related content beyond what the question requires, potentially reaching the classes the specification explicitly prohibits from crossing TB5: recovery tokens, identity-verification secrets, and private account data outside approved context; no minimisation, redaction or classification gate is represented between the assistant's context assembly and the egress flow.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A user asks an ordinary account question; the context assembled behind it over-includes verification-adjacent and recovery-related data, the content leaves the application trust boundary on DF12, and it is processed in the provider's environment with no application-side control over scope.
Security_Impact: Exposure of account, recovery and potentially verification-adjacent information — and of the explicitly prohibited classes, recovery tokens and identity-verification secrets, if scope control fails — to an external party without the user's direct awareness, with regulatory and data protection consequences, and with the data then subject to the provider-side persistence analysed in S3-RT-022.
Architectural_Evidence: TB5 is drawn in this architecture precisely because prompts and contextual information leave the application trust boundary, and the specification states explicitly that the external LLM must never receive recovery tokens, identity-verification secrets or private account data outside approved context, which makes the egress scope a stated security property with no represented enforcement gate. OWASP LLM02 applies and MITRE ATLAS AML.T0024 records exfiltration through the external inference interface; the distinguishing property is that the flow is by design, so the threat is a scope-of-delivery problem rather than an attacker-initiated breach, and it is the only confidentiality loss in the model with no application-side remedy after the fact.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-21, retained and extended to test the specification's explicit egress prohibitions: recovery tokens, identity-verification secrets and private account data outside approved context must never reach EE2, and this entry is the failure mode in which prompt and context assembly lets exactly those classes cross TB5. Retained separately from S3-RT-016, which is interception of the leg, and from S3-RT-022, which is provider-side persistence, because the disclosure here is the intended delivery itself, unchecked in scope. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Provider-side retention, logging and reuse of account data
Affected_Components: EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Context information sent to the LLM; user AI questions
Attack_Mechanism: Conditional provider-side risk: if the external provider retains, logs or reuses for its own purposes the data transmitted on DF12 — practices outside the application's technical control and not specified by the architecture — that content later surfaces through provider incidents, disclosures or lawful access, without any attacker action inside the application.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Data transmitted on DF12 is retained or reused by the provider under practices the application neither sees nor controls; a later provider incident or disclosure exposes the account-related questions and context of the application's users, with no application-side containment possible once the data is in the provider's custody.
Security_Impact: Long-horizon disclosure of account-related questions and context, and loss of control over recovery-related user data after it has crossed TB5, with exposure that cannot be bounded by any application-side containment once the data is in the provider's custody.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM02 extends to the provider's data handling, and the architecture models EE2 as a bare external entity outside application security control with no contractual, technical or retention controls represented; the threat materialises through ordinary provider behaviour rather than through compromise, which distinguishes it from S3-RT-029. Severity is Medium because direct harm requires a secondary event, but the entry is retained because the application's recovery-domain data makes the exposure consequential when it occurs, and because no drawn control addresses it.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-22, retained with conditional scoping: provider-side retention, logging and reuse are practices outside the application's technical control and not specified by the architecture, so the entry is stated conditionally on the provider engaging in them. Retained separately from S3-RT-029, in which the provider is compromised, because here the provider behaves legitimately and the exposure is a custody property. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Cross-user account information leakage through assistant context assembly
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User account information; context information sent to the LLM; generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: If the assembly of the approved contextual information for DF11 over-includes or mis-scopes account data — context belonging to other accounts, or data the requesting user is not authorised to see — the provider's response on DF13 and DF14 faithfully incorporates that context and DF15 delivers it to the wrong user; the architecture draws no authorisation element or context-acquisition flow for the assembly step.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Two users question the assistant; the context assembled for one user's prompt includes account data belonging to another, the generated response incorporates it, and DF15 delivers other users' account and recovery-related information to the requester with the interface's authority.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised disclosure of other users' account and recovery-related information through the assistant interface, in a recovery system potentially including verification-adjacent data that sharpens the targeted takeover attacks S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002.
Architectural_Evidence: The qualifier approved in the description of DF11 implies an authorisation decision inside the context assembly step, yet no authorisation component and no flow for context acquisition is modelled, so the decision has no represented enforcement point; the gap is exactly where cross-user leakage arises, and the entry is absence-justified in the same manner as S3-RT-020, which shares the unmodelled path. Research on LLM-integrated applications records cross-session and cross-user context bleed as a recurring leakage class, and OWASP Top 10 A01 covers the underlying broken object-level authorisation failure.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-23, retained with conditional framing on the unmodelled context-assembly step, absence-justified in the same manner as S3-RT-020. Retained separately from S3-RT-021, in which legitimately scoped context is disclosed to the provider, because here the disclosure is to the wrong user and the control is context authorisation rather than egress minimisation. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Extraction of privileged assistant instructions and prompt content
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Privileged assistant instructions; prompt content; context-handling rules
Attack_Mechanism: If the prompt constructed for the DF11 and DF12 crossings carries privileged instructions or fixed configuration — operating procedures, context-handling rules, workflow detail — crafted questions, direct extraction requests, multi-turn priming or induced rule recitation can cause that content to be reproduced in responses on DF15.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Over several turns an attacker requests verbatim repetition, summaries and rephrasing variants until privileged prompt content and any fixed context appear in a response on DF15, revealing the assistant's instructions and any configuration embedded in them.
Security_Impact: Disclosure of internal design and procedural detail that sharpens the recovery attacks S3-RT-001 and S3-RT-002, enables more convincing social engineering through S3-RT-026, and assists further prompt injection crafting against S3-RT-019 and S3-RT-020.
Architectural_Evidence: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0056 records extraction of LLM prompt content as a distinct technique, and OWASP LLM07 covers prompt leakage; the architecture represents prompt construction at P5 but no distinct instruction element, so the presence of privileged prompt content is conditional on the implementation embedding it, and extraction requires conversation only, no component compromise. Severity is Medium because the loss is informational and primarily enables other entries.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-24, retained and reframed in this review: the supplied architecture represents prompt construction at P5 but no distinct instruction element, so the entry is restated as extraction of privileged assistant instructions and prompt content, conditional on such content being embedded in the constructed prompt. Retained separately from S3-RT-019, the injection that often carries it, because a perfectly injection-resistant assistant can still be induced to reveal configuration through ordinary conversational means, and the mitigations, content policies versus keeping security-relevant logic out of prompts, differ. Primary STRIDE is Information Disclosure.

Threat_Name: Hallucinated account recovery guidance
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: The external provider generates plausible but false recovery guidance on DF13 — non-existent steps, wrong verification channels, fabricated contact routes or incorrect procedural detail — which the assistant relays on DF14 and P1 displays on DF15 with the interface's apparent authority and no factual validation step in between.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A locked-out user asks how to recover their account; the generated guidance confidently describes a procedure that does not exist or directs verification answers to a wrong channel, the response is displayed as an ordinary answer, and the user follows it.
Security_Impact: Users following incorrect recovery procedures: failed recoveries, disclosure of verification data to wrong channels, and priming for phishing that impersonates the fabricated procedures, in the workflow where users are least able to judge correctness because they are locked out and dependent on guidance.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM09 identifies misinformation, and the 2023 edition's LLM09 overreliance framing already tied generation errors to user harm; hallucination is an intrinsic generation failure mode that no component in this architecture validates, since DF14 and DF15 carry the response to display without any accuracy control. Account recovery is the highest-stakes guidance context this system offers, which is what elevates an otherwise generic LLM weakness into an architecture-relevant entry.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-25, retained. The entry absorbs the user-trust amplification formerly carried by the excluded excessive-trust entry: users mid-recovery are locked out and dependent on guidance and cannot easily validate what they are told, which amplifies this entry's impact but is not a distinct mechanism. Retained separately from S3-RT-026 because hallucination is factual error produced without attacker intent, whereas unsafe advice is content harmful if followed regardless of its origin, and only the latter is mitigated by content policy; both can co-occur in one response. Per the review's mandated distinction, incorrect guidance here is not a recovery-authority bypass. Primary STRIDE is Tampering under an explicitly extended interpretation, loss of integrity of generated information.

Threat_Name: Unsafe AI-generated advice undermining account security
Affected_Components: P4 AI Account Support Assistant
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: Generated responses displayed on DF15 contain advice that actively undermines security — encouraging users to share verification answers through the chat, describing workaround steps around recovery controls, or directing users to external channels and contact points — whether the content originates in hallucination through S3-RT-025, injection through S3-RT-019 and S3-RT-020, or provider compromise through S3-RT-029.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: A user mid-recovery asks the assistant for help; the displayed answer advises sharing verification answers in the conversation or following an external contact route, the user complies because the instruction arrives inside the trusted application in direct response to their own question, and the account is compromised with the user's own participation.
Security_Impact: Users persuaded into self-compromising actions during the most sensitive account workflow: verification data disclosed to attacker-influenced channels, recovery controls circumvented by cooperative victims, and account takeover completed with the user's own participation.
Architectural_Evidence: Research on LLM-integrated applications records unsafe advice in safety-relevant contexts as a failure class distinct from factual error: the content is actionable, authoritative in presentation, and harmful when followed, and the assistant is this system's user-facing guidance channel with no human-authored content control represented between generation on DF13 and display on DF15. The stated assistant limitations bound what the advice can directly execute, but they do not bound what the advice can persuade a user to do, which is why severity is High.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-26, retained. The entry likewise absorbs the user-trust amplification formerly carried by the excluded excessive-trust entry, the recovery context making cooperative victims the norm rather than the exception. Retained separately from S3-RT-025 per the mechanism distinction stated there. Per the review's mandated distinction, unsafe guidance here is not a recovery-authority bypass; only the P2-path entries deliver that. Primary STRIDE is Tampering.

Threat_Name: Insecure output handling: active content in assistant responses
Affected_Components: P1 Web Frontend
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated AI responses; recovery tokens
Attack_Mechanism: Generated content arriving on DF14 and displayed on DF15 contains active content that P1 presents without content separation or handling safeguards — none is specified on the display path — and that executes in the user's client context; an attacker seeds the content through injection S3-RT-019 or S3-RT-020, or through provider compromise S3-RT-029, none of which the rendering path can distinguish.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: Through injection or provider compromise the attacker induces the model to emit active content in its answer; P1 displays the response as content with execution capability, it runs in the user's client context, captures session state and any recovery token handled in the same context, and hands off to S3-RT-003 for account takeover.
Security_Impact: Client-side compromise inside the application context: theft of session state and of any recovery token handled in the same client context, handing off to S3-RT-003 for account takeover, and execution of actions in the victim's name.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM05 requires treating model output as untrusted input, and A5 of the supplied assumptions declares it so; the architecture carries generated content from beyond TB5 through DF13 and DF14 straight to display at P1 with no content-handling element specified, and the display context is the recovery workflow itself, where valid tokens can be present in the same client context, which is what makes the chain to account takeover direct rather than theoretical.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-27, retained with an architecture-only rewrite: rendering and encoding mechanisms were generalised to content separation and handling safeguards on the display path, none being specified. This entry is the practical realisation of unintended AI authority in this architecture: generated content becomes executable in the client context, which is how the excessive-authority concern manifests when the assistant itself is structurally unprivileged under A3 and A4. Retained separately from S3-RT-013, whose content originates in stored profile and recovery data, because the source here is the LLM chain and the control must sit on the DF14 to DF15 display path specifically. Primary STRIDE is Tampering.

Threat_Name: Compromise or substitution of the external LLM provider
Affected_Components: EE2 External LLM Provider; P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated AI responses; context information sent to the LLM
Attack_Mechanism: The DF12/DF13 exchange depends on the identity and integrity of the responder beyond TB5, and no mechanism verifying that the responder is the intended external provider is specified by the architecture; if EE2 is substituted or compromised, prompts and account-related context are harvested and every response is attacker-controlled.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The communication that P5 sends on DF12 is answered by an attacker-controlled replacement of the intended provider, the substitution path lying outside the drawn architecture; every question and account-related context submission is harvested, and every DF13 response is attacker-authored, weaponising the guidance entries S3-RT-025 and S3-RT-026 and the output-handling entry S3-RT-027 for all users.
Security_Impact: Interception of every prompt and account-related context submission crossing TB5 together with control of every response returned on DF13, converting the assistant into an attacker-controlled channel for all users.
Architectural_Evidence: P5 is the only element that performs the TB5 crossing, so any verification of the external provider's identity and integrity must concentrate at that single component, and no such verification is specified; EE2 is not merely a service the application calls but the source of content the application displays to users on DF15. OWASP LLM03 applies, and MITRE ATLAS frames the substitution angle as ML supply chain compromise.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-29, retained with a STRIDE collapse and a trust-boundary-level rewrite: primary Spoofing, the trusted external entity impersonated or substituted, with control of the responses (tampering) and harvesting of submissions (information disclosure) noted as consequences; infrastructure-specific substitution mechanisms were removed per the architecture-only scope. Retained separately from S3-RT-022, in which the provider behaves legitimately but retains data, and from S3-RT-017, in which the application's own credential is lost, because here the provider itself is the compromised party and the mitigation class is provider assurance and response validation rather than secrets hygiene.

Threat_Name: Denial of service on the Account Recovery Service
Affected_Components: P2 Account Recovery Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Session/account recovery state; user account information
Attack_Mechanism: An attacker floods the recovery interface on DF1 and DF2 with automated requests; each request triggers verification lookups on DF3 and DF4 and potentially token operations on DF5 and DF6, saturating the service and its database capacity so that legitimate locked-out users cannot complete recovery.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits recovery requests at high volume; every request costs verification lookups and potential token operations, the service's capacity is consumed, and legitimate locked-out users cannot complete recovery for the duration.
Security_Impact: Recovery denied to legitimate users at the moment of highest need, a lockout condition that also functions as extortion pressure, degrades trust in the platform, and masks concurrent targeted attacks from S3-RT-001 through S3-RT-006 in the resulting noise.
Architectural_Evidence: STRIDE assigns denial of service to boundary-exposed processing, and the recovery workflow is inherently reachable by unauthenticated users because its purpose is to serve users who have lost credentials, so it cannot simply be gated behind authentication; the architecture models no rate limiting, queueing or load isolation for DF2. High severity reflects that the service's entire purpose is availability of access restoration: denying it locks affected users out of their accounts as surely as a takeover, without needing to defeat any control.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-30, retained. The recovery workflow is inherently unauthenticated by purpose, and no throttling or load isolation is drawn. Retained separately from S3-RT-031, which targets the token store's state volume rather than service capacity. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service.

Threat_Name: Recovery token generation abuse and token store exhaustion
Affected_Components: DS2 Recovery Token Storage; P2 Account Recovery Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Recovery tokens; session/account recovery state
Attack_Mechanism: The attacker drives mass token generation through high-volume recovery requests that pass or bypass preliminary checks, so that active tokens and status records accumulate in DS2 through DF5 without any modelled quota, expiry sweep or lifecycle management, inflating the store and increasing contention on the validation lookups of DF6.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker triggers token issuance at scale; active tokens and status records accumulate in DS2 with no drawn quota or lifecycle management, storage grows, and validation lookups on DF6 contend with the accumulated state, degrading or denying token validation for legitimate recoveries.
Security_Impact: Degraded or denied token validation for legitimate recoveries, storage exhaustion on DS2, and operational cost, converting the recovery state store into a resource exhaustion vector distinct from the service flooding of S3-RT-030.
Architectural_Evidence: Architecture-specific analysis of the token lifecycle the model draws: DF5 shows unbounded generation into DS2 and DF6 shows validation reads against it, with no quota, sweep or lifecycle management represented, and TB4 exists because that state is sensitive authentication state; abuse at the token layer therefore attacks the store and the validation path rather than the service's request capacity. Severity is Medium because the effect is degradation that grows over time and because the natural mitigations, per-account and per-issuer throttling, also serve S3-RT-002 and S3-RT-030.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-31, retained with a technology-neutral rewording of the lifecycle examples. Retained separately from S3-RT-030, whose vector and target are the request handling capacity of P2 itself. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service.

Threat_Name: External LLM provider unavailability
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service; EE2 External LLM Provider
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Generated AI responses
Attack_Mechanism: The external provider suffers outage, rate limiting or degraded service, so that DF13 returns errors or nothing, P5 cannot produce processed responses on DF14, and the assistant delivers no answers on DF15 for any user of the application.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: The external provider suffers an extended outage; DF13 responses never arrive, and the assistant returns errors or nothing to every user, while core recovery and profile flows continue unaffected.
Security_Impact: AI assistant functionality lost application-wide, removing the system's guidance channel precisely for users mid-recovery; core recovery and profile flows on DF1 through DF9 continue unaffected, which bounds the blast radius to the assistant's auxiliary role.
Architectural_Evidence: Architecture-specific dependency analysis: all assistant functionality routes through a single external entity beyond TB5 with no modelled fallback, degradation strategy or second provider, so the availability of a user-facing feature is ceded to a third party, and the entry is AI-specific because the dependency is an LLM service. The explicit bounding of impact is part of the analysis: unlike S3-RT-030, which denies the recovery service itself, this entry denies the auxiliary channel, which is why severity is Medium.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-32, retained. The bounded blast radius is part of the architectural analysis and is why severity is Medium. Retained separately from S3-RT-033, in which the attacker deliberately consumes the provider relationship. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service.

Threat_Name: Unbounded LLM consumption through automated assistant abuse
Affected_Components: P5 LLM Integration Service
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: User AI questions; context information sent to the LLM
Attack_Mechanism: An attacker automates question submission on DF10, which requires no identity verification per S3-RT-010, driving unbounded provider calls on DF12 with maximal context attached, and exhausting usage quotas, budgets and possibly the provider relationship itself.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker automates the submission of context-heavy questions at high frequency on DF10; each question drives a DF12 crossing whose cost scales with the question and the attached context, the provider quota and budget exhaust, and the assistant is denied to legitimate users through billing rather than capacity.
Security_Impact: Financial exhaustion of the provider arrangement, rate limit starvation that denies the assistant to legitimate users and compounds S3-RT-032, and potential contractual suspension of the external service on which all assistant functionality depends.
Architectural_Evidence: OWASP LLM10 identifies unbounded consumption as a top ten LLM application risk: the architecture models no metering, quota or cost control anywhere on the DF10 to DF12 chain, and the unauthenticated entry point established by S3-RT-010 removes even attribution for abuse, so neither prevention nor accounting is represented. The entry is AI-specific because the cost driver is usage-scaled model inference, growing with question and context volume, a property of LLM services with no analogue in the classical flows of this architecture.
Expert_Justification: Catalogue entry T-33, retained with a technology-neutral rewording of the cost driver. Retained separately from S3-RT-032, in which the provider fails on its own, and from S3-RT-030, in which the target is the application's own service, because here the attacker deliberately spends a third-party resource the application has undertaken to pay for. Primary STRIDE is Denial of Service.

Threat_Name: Profile updates performed without valid recovery authorisation
Affected_Components: P3 Profile Management Service; P2 Account Recovery Service
Affected_Data_Flows: DF8, DF9 (the authorisation precondition's enforcement point is not represented in the model)
Affected_Asset_Security_Property: Profile information; user account information; integrity of the recovery-authorisation precondition
Attack_Mechanism: The architecture states that P3 performs updates only after authorised recovery approval, but no flow or element shows how P3 establishes that approval: no P2-to-P3 authorisation flow is drawn, and no consultation of DS2's token state by P3 is represented. If the implementation accepts update requests on DF8 without verifiable proof of a valid recovery authorisation, profile modification is available without the recovery the precondition exists to enforce.
Concrete_Attack_Scenario: An attacker submits a profile update request on DF8 with no completed recovery behind it — the authorisation precondition absent, forged, or merely asserted in the request; P3 persists the change to DS1 on DF9, and the modification stands although no recovery was ever authorised for the account.
Security_Impact: Unauthorised profile modification that bypasses the recovery-authorisation gate entirely, collapsing the stated ordering — recovery first, update after — and arming the downstream paths that manipulated profile data enables, including S3-RT-013 and the recovery arming of S3-RT-008.
Architectural_Evidence: A1 makes P2 the only recovery authorisation authority, and the supplied architecture makes authorised recovery approval the stated precondition of every P3 update, yet the model draws neither a flow conveying that approval to P3 nor any P3-side check of it; a stated security property without a represented enforcement point is an architecture-level gap the reference model must record, in the same manner as the token-redemption binding gap of S3-RT-006.
Expert_Justification: NEW ENTRY added in this review. Reason: the profile-management checklist requires coverage of modification without valid recovery authorisation, and the catalogue's existing profile entries attack record selection (S3-RT-007), field scope (S3-RT-008) and store access (S3-RT-009) but not the precondition itself; the mechanism here is the missing enforcement of the recovery-authorisation gate at P3, which is distinct from all three and admits a distinct mitigation, verifiable authorisation proof bound to the update request. Absence-justified rather than drawn-flow-justified, hence Confidence Medium. Primary STRIDE is Elevation of Privilege: a protected capability is exercised without entitlement. Severity High; Likelihood Medium. Not LLM-specific.
